How to use this book How to use this book This workbook provides questions for you to practise what you have learned in class. There is a unit to match each unit in your Learner’s Book. Writing tip Tips to help you with your learning. Use shortened sentences in adverts You Must be able to do experiments. Experience needed … Use of English We can use the present perfect to talk about indefinite time in the past. My dad has visited many countries, but he hasn’t been to China. today (dad has visited many countries up to now) past We often use adverbs with the present perfect too. We use yet to mean any time up to now. Have you ﬁ nished your lunch yet? We use ever in questions to talk about an experience up to the present. Have you ever had a scary experience? We use just to talk about the recent past. Yes, I’ve just seen a spider in the cupboard. Get it right! Remember to use the correct spelling. musn’t mustn’t shoud should Focus 1 Find out about the history of the telephone. Complete the text with verbs in the past simple. Alexander Graham Bell is known for inventing the telephone in the late 1800s. He was (be) born in Scotland in 1847 and 2 (become) interested 1 in the science of sound because both his mother and wife 3 (be) deaf. He loved doing experiments and eventually he was able to send voice signals down a telephone wire. The first telephone call 4 (take) place in March 1876 between Alexander Graham Bell and his assistant Thomas Watson. The telephone he 5 (use) was tall and long and you 6 (have) to use a separate mouth and ear piece, one to listen and one to speak. As design developed people 7 (begin) to use a round dial with numbers. Now we use wireless phones, which let us talk and move around the house at the same time. Information to help you find out more about grammar. Use the Cambridge Learner Corpus to get your grammar right! Each Use of English lesson is divided into three parts: Focus: these grammar questions help you to master the basics. 6 Original material © Cambridge University Press 2021. This material is not final and is subject to further changes prior to publication. ISBN_9781108810906.

Practice 2 Kofi has saved his pocket money and wants to buy a new football shirt. Circle and number the eight errors in the conversation, then write the corrections at the end. Kofi: There’s the City shirt and the National kit. I don’t know which one to buy! Dad: Well, which one will you wear the oftenest, do you think? 1 Kofi: The City shirt, because we go to City games all the time … but I like the National shirt more better! Dad: OK, but I think that shirt costs much than the other one. Have you checked? Kofi: Oh yes, it’s more expensive. I think I’ve got enough pocket money … Dad: OK then, try them both on. Let’s see which one fits the better. [Kofi tries on the two shirts]. Kofi: The National shirt definitely fits the best but it costs the more! I don’t know what to do! Dad: Mmm … and the City shirt is a bit too big – it fits more looser, but that is a good thing because you are growing more faster this year than ever before! Kofi: So the City shirt will last the most longest? We are working with Cambridge Assessment International Education towards endorsement of this title. 1 My world 1.3 Prepositions before nouns Use of English We use prepositions to show the connection between nouns and adjectives in a sentence. Common prepositions are on, in, at, from. 1 Location At: speciﬁ c locations, addresses, shops, events I’m at Wei’s house. Ellie isn’t at the party. On: single mountains, planets, beaches, islands, public transport I get to school on the bus. I’m on Mount Everest. In: buildings, cities, countries, continents, groups of people I couldn’t see Anna in the crowd. Do you live in Italy? 2 Origin I’m from Indonesia. Latitude lines circle the Earth from east to west. Focus 1 Read about Eva’s incredible holiday. Circle the correct preposition in each sentence. a I had an amazing holiday in / on Asia. b We flew to / from London, Heathrow, to Bangkok. c On / From the airport terminal, we got in / on the bus to the city centre. d We stayed at / on Paradise Point hotel on a main street in the city. We visited all the sights from / in the city. e f One day, I got lost on / in a crowd of people, but my dad quickly found me! 12 Original material © Cambridge University Press 2021. We are working with Cambridge Assessment International Education towards endorsement of this title. 2 Sport 2.2 1st conditional with if/unless Use of English We use the first conditional to talk about situations in the future which we think are possible. The if clause tells you the condition. The main clause tells you the result. If you exercise, you’ll feel good. We can use the main clause first but this doesn’t change the meaning. We always use a comma if the if clause is first. If you practise every day, you’ll win. You’ll win if you practise every day. We can use unless instead of if. It’s the same as if not. Unless you practise every day, you won’t win. Focus 1 Rita has got a big gymnastics competition next month. Read and circle the correct word in each sentence. If she trains / will train hard, she’ll do / do well in the competition. a b Unless she eats / eat well, she will / won’t have any energy. c She will be / is in tip-top condition, if she will train / trains hard. If she is / will be worried, she’ll / won’t talk to her coach. d e She’ll / won’t perform well if she sleeps / doesn’t sleep well before the competition. If she feels / will feel nervous before the competition, she’ll need / needs to f breathe deeply. 22 Original material © Cambridge University Press 2021. This material is not final and is subject to further changes prior to publication. ISBN_9781108810906.

We are working with Cambridge Assessment International Education towards endorsement of this title. 2 Sport 2.3 need / should / mustn’t for advice Use of English We use need + infinitive with to, to express something that is necessary. You need to train hard to win the race. We use should to give advice. We use should + infinitive without to. You should stretch your muscles after exercise. We use must + infinitive without to, to give strong advice against something. You mustn’t eat just before you do exercise. Focus 1 Read Omer’s running tips. Circle the correct word in each sentence. You need / mustn’t run without warming up first. a b When you warm up, you need / should stretch your muscles too. c You should / mustn’t force your muscles when you stretch or you might hurt yourself. You need / must to have good trainers or you’ll d get injured. e You mustn’t / don’t need to drink water while you are running, but you should / mustn’t drink water before. You mustn’t / should run too fast to begin with or you won’t finish the race. f 24 Original material © Cambridge University Press 2021. This material is not final and is subject to further changes prior to publication. ISBN_9781108810906.

Do you know the names of any famous basketball players? 2 Read the biography of Lebron James. Match the headings 1–4 to the paragraphs A–D. 1 His journey to stardom 2 Present-day success 3 Information about his childhood 4 Amazing facts! A Lebron James is one of the best players in basketball today. In 2018 he signed a four-year deal with the Los Angeles Lakers for $154 million. He is known for his amazing leaping ability, height and strength. B He was born in Akron, Ohio, USA, on 30 December 1984. His family life was difficult because his father disappeared when he was young and his family didn’t have much money. He studied at St Vincent–St Mary High School in Ohio and helped his team win three state titles. He earned the name ‘Mr Basketball’ for his incredible talent. C After leaving college early, Lebron joined the NBA’s Cleveland Cavaliers and became a star overnight! He helped the Miami Heat to win titles in 2012 and 2013, and when he moved back to Cleveland he led the team to its first championship title in 2016 before joining the Lakers in 2018. We can use different time expressions. he 1 A definite point in time: in 2020, last week, yesterday, a month ago In 2014, Asimo played football with a US president. 2 An indefinite point in time: when she was a child, a long time ago, the other day Scientists created Asimo a long time ago in order to help people in need. Regular verbs are formed by adding -ed, -d or ied: started, created, carried Irregular verbs do not follow a rule. The first telephone call 4 (take) place in March 1876 between Alexander Graham Bell and his assistant Thomas Watson. The telephone he 5 (use) was tall and long and you 6 (have) to use a separate mouth and ear piece, one to listen and one to speak. As design developed people 7 (begin) to use a round dial with numbers. Now we use wireless phones, which let us talk and move around the house at the same time. 46 Original material © Cambridge University Press 2021. We are working with Cambridge Assessment International Education towards endorsement of this title. 5 Money 5.2 Comparative and superlative adverbs Use of English We can use comparative adverbs to show change or compare how something is done. He grows out of them less quickly than me. She works harder than everyone else. We can also use superlative adverbs to make comparisons. I spend my pocket money fastest in the shopping mall! We go shopping most often at the weekend. To make a superlative adverb stronger, we often use the + superlative adverb. This brand of sportswear always sells the best because it lasts the longest. Base adverb Comparative Superlative 1 syllable: fast hard faster harder (the) fastest (the) hardest more / less quickly 2 syllables: quickly often more / less often (the) most / least quickly (the ) most / least often Irregular: well badly better worse (the) best (the) worst Focus 1 The Ruiz family have saved and bought a camper van for holidays. We are working with Cambridge Assessment International Education towards endorsement of this title. 5 Money 5.3 Quantifiers Use of English We use the quantifiers, several and plenty of, to describe amounts of things (we don’t know exactly how much). At the school fair, there were several book stalls… (several = 3 or 4) … and there were plenty of food stalls… (plenty of = lots of) Either … or and both of always refer to ‘two’. Either ... or means a choice of two. both or both of = two people or things Both comes after the verb, to be; but before other verbs: You are both very good at helping … We both baked cakes for the school fair. You can either help with the book stall or tidy up the rubbish – it’s up to you! neither … nor = the negative form of either … or (‘not either’) There’s neither burgers nor sausages at the school fair – most of the food is vegetarian. We are working with Cambridge Assessment International Education towards endorsement of this title. 6 People and work 6.2 Adjectives + prepositions + nouns Use of English Some adjectives and preposition always go together. There are no fixed rules, so it helps to learn the words together, as a ‘chunk’. Adjective + preposition phrases are often followed by a noun (or pronoun). Here are some patterns to help you remember (but remember that there are exceptions). We use (adjective +) at, for skills and abilities. I was good at maths and science anyway. I worked hard at them at school. We use about and of to talk about feelings. Ben is nervous about his maths exam. Hua is proud of her science project. We can also use adjectives with in and with. For this job, you need to be experiencedin photography. He is great with engines and machines. Focus 1 Read about Lisa, a chocolate expert. Circle the correct prepositions. To do Lisa’s job, you must be very enthusiastic 3 about / in the product because you have to persuade people to buy it! You must be good 4 of / with people and enjoy talking to them about the different types of chocolate. As a child, Lisa was very fond 5 of / about deserts and she loved cooking and baking. When she was a teenager, she tried making her own chocolate (not easy!). She soon realised that she was more interested 6 with / in chocolate than any other sweet treat and she decided then that she wanted to become a chocolate expert! 2 Read the text again and underline the noun or pronoun that follows each adjective + preposition phrase. 70 Original material © Cambridge University Press 2021. Language focus: could (+verb) In these sentences, we use could (+ verb) to talk about something that is possible. You could be a doctor and look after the sick. We use couldn’t (+ verb) to talk about something that isn’t possible. She couldn’t learn to drive – she isn’t old enough.

We are working with Cambridge Assessment International Education towards endorsement of this title. 7 Nature’s power 7.2 Past simple and past continuous Use of English We use the past continuous to describe actions happening at the same time as another action in the past. The other action is usually in the past simple. We were making a ﬁ lm in Indonesia when the volcano suddenly exploded. We make the past continuous with the past form of the verb, be (was / were) + verb + -ing. We can use linking words, when, as, while. While everything seemed normal outside, magma was rising inside the volcano. People were escaping from their homes as the volcano erupted. We make the negative form with wasn’t / weren’t (was / were not). I wasn’t playing in the park when the lightning struck, I was at home. Luckily we weren’t standing too close when the explosion happened. Questions Where were you going when you saw the ash cloud? Was she working nearby while the eruption happened? Yes, he was / No, he wasn’t. Focus film watch do 1 What did Tara see when she watched a news story about a volcanic explosion? We are working with Cambridge Assessment International Education towards endorsement of this title. 7 Nature’s power 7.3 Connecting words Use of English Connecting words join two parts of a sentence and show when something happens. Don’t move from where you are while the earthquake is happening. (at the same time as) As soon as the shaking starts get down on your hands and knees. (immediately after) Stay inside until the shaking stops. (a point in time) We use before and after to talk about the order of events in the past or future. Make sure you know what to do before an earthquake happens. After an earthquake happens, there is usually a lot of damage. We can put as soon as, before and after at the beginning of a sentence and in the middle. We usually put while and until in the middle (but sometimes at the beginning too). You can go outside as soon as the storm stops. While it’s raining so hard, you should stay inside. Focus 1 What should you do during a strong lightning storm? We are working with Cambridge Assessment International Education towards endorsement of this title. 8 Entertainment 8.2 Past simple passive Use of English We use passive to talk about past events. We use it when we want to focus on the event, not the person who did it. We make the past simple passive with the past form of the verb be (was / were) + past participle. These early ﬁ lms were made in black and white. If we want to mention the person who did the action, we use by. y . In 1891, the ﬁ rst ﬁ lm projector was invented by the Edison company. We make the negative form with wasn’t / weren’t (was / were not) + past participle. Sound wasn’t added to ﬁ lms until the 1920s. We use question word + was / were + past participle to make questions. uestions What was the ﬁ rst animated ﬁ lm called? We use was / were + past participle to make yes / no questions. Was the ﬁ rst cinema opened in 1905? Yes, it was. We are working with Cambridge Assessment International Education towards endorsement of this title. 8 Entertainment 8.3 Adverbs of time and frequency Use of English These adverbs describe when an action happens. Some adverbs can describe definite (exact) time: We’ve talked today about what you do on your devices. Definite adverbs such as yesterday, today, tonight and tomorrow often go at the beginning or end of the sentence. Tomorrow you can play video games, but not now. We didn’t have any screen time yesterday. Definite adverbs such as hourly, daily, weekly (that measure time) go at the end of a sentence. How much time do you spend on your tablet weekly? Some adverbs don’t specify an exact time (indefinite adverbs): I often use my tablet for schoolwork. Indefinite adverbs usually go after the pronoun and before the main verb in a sentence or question. BUT the adverb goes after the pronoun and the verb to be. We sometimes use a Maths website to help with our homework. He is always on his phone! We are working with Cambridge Assessment International Education towards endorsement of this title. 9 Amazing arts 9.2 Present perfect for unfinished past Use of English The present perfect can be used to talk about the unfinished past. It connects a past situation to the present in some way. I’ve had two music classesthis week. (‘this week’ hasn’t ﬁ nished yet) It is also used to talk about an indefinite time in the past. I’ve made my sculpture out of recycled objects. (recent ‘indeﬁ nite’ past) While in contrast we use the past simple to talk about a definite time in the past. Yesterday, I made a wind instrument called a kazoo. Definite time Focus 1 Read the text about recycled art. Use the verbs in the box to complete the text. Use the present perfect. We are working with Cambridge Assessment International Education towards endorsement of this title. 9 Amazing arts 9.3 Present tenses with future meaning Use of English Present tenses with future meaning We use the present simple for events in the future which are certain because they are facts, or because there is a fixed schedule. Their train leaves early on Wednesday morning … The new school term doesn’t start until September. What time does the museum close in the summer? We can use the present continuous to talk about the future. It shows that we have already decided something and that we have already made a plan or arrangements. They are arriving on Sunday and staying until Wednesday. Dom is meeting his cousin next week for a day out. They aren’t visiting the sculpture park at the weekend anymore. They’ve changed their plans. What are you doing on Thursday? I’m going to see the Star Circus.
